chapter.title: Introduction to Neural Networks
chapter.description: Layers, activations, parameters, data splits, one-hidden-layer lab

questions.q: A neural network with an input layer, one hidden layer and one output layer is called a 2-layer neural network.
questions.explain: The input layer is not counted. Layers counted = hidden layers + output layer, so 1 + 1 = 2.

questions.q: A network with 10 hidden layers that all use the linear activation g(z) = z is more powerful than a single linear layer.
questions.explain: The composition of linear functions is linear: W[2]W[1]x + W[2]b[1] + b[2] = W'x + b'. Depth adds nothing without non-linearity, so the network is equivalent to one linear layer.

questions.q: The output range of ReLU is (-1, 1).
questions.explain: ReLU(z) = max(0, z) gives values in [0, +∞). The range (-1, 1) belongs to tanh, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.q: The derivative of tanh can be written 1 - a², where a = tanh(z).
questions.explain: This is the formula used in backprop: the term (1 - A[1]²) in dZ[1] is the tanh derivative.

questions.q: Initializing all weights W to zero is acceptable as long as the biases are random.
questions.explain: It is the opposite: biases can safely start at 0, but equal weights make all hidden neurons compute the same thing and receive the same gradient (symmetry problem). Random W breaks the symmetry.

questions.q: The dev set is used to give the final unbiased estimate of performance.
questions.explain: That is the role of the test set. The dev set is used to tune hyperparameters and compare models.

questions.q: When normalizing the test set, you should recompute the mean and variance on the test data.
questions.explain: You must reuse the mean and variance computed on the train set. Recomputing them on test data would apply a different transformation than the one the model was trained with.

questions.q: The number of hidden neurons is a parameter learned during training.
questions.explain: It is a hyperparameter chosen by you before training. Parameters are W and b, which are learned.

questions.q: With small random weights and a sigmoid output, the first cost for binary cross-entropy should be close to 0.693.
questions.explain: Small weights give a[2] ≈ 0.5, so the cost ≈ -log(0.5) ≈ 0.693. This is a useful sanity check.

questions.q: If a model reaches higher training accuracy with more hidden units, this proves it generalizes better.
questions.explain: Accuracy measured on the training set cannot reveal overfitting. A dev set is needed to judge generalization.

questions.q: Dev and test sets should come from the same distribution as the training set.
questions.explain: Training on real cat photos and testing on cartoon cats fails because the data is of a different nature.

questions.q: In the lab, logistic regression reached about 47% accuracy on the flower dataset because the classes are not linearly separable.
questions.explain: A straight line cannot separate the petals, so a hidden layer is needed to build a curved boundary.

questions.q: What are the shapes of W[1] and b[1] for a network with n_x inputs and n_h hidden neurons?
questions.explain: Rows = neurons of the current layer, columns = neurons of the previous layer for W. b has one entry per hidden neuron: (n_h, 1). Option A is the transposed mistake; m (number of examples) never appears in parameter shapes.

questions.q: Which activation is the best choice for the output layer of a binary classifier?
questions.explain: Sigmoid outputs a value in (0, 1) that can be read as a probability. Tanh could give negative values, and ReLU/Leaky ReLU are unbounded.

questions.q: What is dZ[2] for a sigmoid output with cross-entropy loss?
questions.explain: Combining the sigmoid derivative with the cross-entropy derivative simplifies to A[2] - Y. Option A is only the sigmoid derivative, without the loss part.

questions.q: Which hyperparameter set is correct?
options: Learning rate, number of hidden layers, number of iterations
questions.explain: Hyperparameters are chosen by you before training. W and b are learned parameters, and J/accuracy are measurements.

questions.q: With 1,000,000 examples, which split is considered enough according to the course?
questions.explain: With huge data, 1% dev and 1% test already contain 10,000 examples each. The classic 60/20/20 split wastes data that could be used for training.

questions.q: Why did ReLU perform worst in the lab with n_h = 4 and small initialization?
options: ReLU cannot be used in hidden layers
Tiny weights leave many units inactive, and with few units its piecewise linear boundary cannot form the petals
ReLU always needs a learning rate above 1
questions.explain: Small weights (x0.01) give many units with output 0 and gradient 0, and 4 piecewise linear units give too few line segments. ReLU is a fine hidden activation in deep networks, so option A is wrong.

questions.q: In the lab, what happens with learning rate 0.01 and 5000 iterations, versus 50000 iterations?
options: 58.5% with 5000 and 88% with 50000: it is slow, not bad
It reaches 90% with 5000 and then overfits
questions.explain: A small learning rate means very small steps, so the cost barely moves. With 10x more iterations it catches up to about 88%.

questions.q: Why is keepdims=True used in np.sum(dZ2, axis=1, keepdims=True)?
options: To keep the shape (n, 1) instead of (n,), avoiding broadcasting bugs
To compute the sum over the examples as a scalar
To convert the result to a list
questions.explain: Without it, the result has shape (n,), which can broadcast incorrectly with (n, 1) arrays.

questions.q: In Xavier and He initialization, which pairing is correct?
options: Xavier: sqrt(2/n) for ReLU; He: sqrt(1/n) for tanh
Xavier: sqrt(1/n) for tanh/sigmoid; He: sqrt(2/n) for ReLU
questions.explain: Xavier scales weights by sqrt(1/n) (good for tanh/sigmoid) and He by sqrt(2/n) (good for ReLU). Option A swaps them.

questions.q: Which dataset showed that logistic regression is at chance level and a hidden layer is essential, since one class is inside the other?
questions.explain: Logistic regression got 53% on gaussian_quantiles while the hidden layer reached up to 100%. noisy_circles has a similar ring structure but noise caps its accuracy, which is the tempting wrong choice.

questions.q: For the 4-unit flower network, what is the correct forward order?
options: Z1 = W1·X + b1, A1 = tanh(Z1), Z2 = W2·A1 + b2, A2 = sigmoid(Z2)
A1 = tanh(X), Z1 = W1·A1, Z2 = W2·X, A2 = sigmoid(Z1)
Z1 = W1·X, A1 = sigmoid(Z1), Z2 = W2·A1, A2 = tanh(Z2)
Z2 = W2·X + b2, A2 = tanh(Z2), Z1 = W1·A2 + b1, A1 = sigmoid(Z1)
questions.explain: The hidden layer uses tanh and the output layer uses sigmoid, with each Z computed from the previous layer's activations.

questions.q: Which activation functions are non-linear? (select all)
questions.explain: Sigmoid, tanh and Leaky ReLU all have a curved or piecewise graph with changing slope. g(z) = z is linear and would collapse the network into one linear layer.

questions.q: Which of these are parameters (learned by training)? (select all)
questions.explain: W and b are learned. The learning rate and number of hidden neurons are hyperparameters you choose.

questions.q: What are the consequences of using a very small learning rate? (select all)
options: The cost stays near its initial value for a long time
The cost oscillates and may diverge
questions.explain: Tiny steps mean slow progress and the need for more iterations. Oscillation and divergence come from a learning rate that is too large.

questions.q: Which statements about the train/dev/test sets are correct? (select all)
options: The dev set is used to tune hyperparameters
The test set gives an unbiased final estimate
Dev and test must come from the same distribution as training
Normalization statistics should be recomputed on the test set
questions.explain: The last statement is wrong: the mean and variance must come from the train set and be reused on dev and test.

questions.q: Which statements about tanh are correct? (select all)
options: Usually better than sigmoid in hidden layers
questions.explain: The derivative a(1 - a) belongs to sigmoid. For tanh it is 1 - a².

questions.q: Which statements explain why the hidden layer size experiments need care? (select all)
options: For n_h ≥ 10 the cost keeps dropping while accuracy stays about 90%
Accuracy on the training set can hide overfitting
n_h = 50 is always the best because the cost is lowest
questions.explain: A lower training cost with more units does not mean better generalization, so option D is wrong. A dev set is needed to judge it.

questions.q: Which are reasons why normalizing input vectors helps? (select all)
options: It removes the need for a test set
questions.explain: Normalization x := (x - μ) / σ gives a rounder cost surface and faster convergence. It has no relation to the need for a test set.

questions.q: Which statements about the dimensions are correct for m examples? (select all)
questions.explain: W[2] has shape (n_y, n_h), not (n_h, n_y): rows are the neurons of the current layer.

questions.q: Why do we need non-linear activation functions in a neural network?
questions.answer: With a linear activation, the composition of layers is still linear (W[2]W[1]x + W[2]b[1] + b[2] = W'x + b'), so the network is equivalent to one linear layer. Non-linearity lets the network learn complex, curved relationships.
questions.explain: Write the two-layer derivation to get full marks.

questions.q: Why must the weights W be initialized randomly, while the biases b can be zero?
questions.answer: If all weights start equal, every hidden neuron computes the same output and gets the same gradient, so they never differ (symmetry problem). Random initialization breaks the symmetry. Biases do not suffer from this, so zeros are fine.
questions.explain: Mention that the random weights are also small (×0.01) to avoid saturation of tanh/sigmoid.

questions.q: Why does a small initialization (×0.01) matter with tanh or sigmoid?
questions.answer: Large weights give large |z|, which falls in the flat parts of the curve where the gradient is tiny, so learning is slow.
questions.explain: This idea is developed in the initialization chapter.

questions.q: Explain the difference between parameters and hyperparameters, and give two examples of each.
questions.answer: Parameters (W[l], b[l]) are learned by training. Hyperparameters (learning rate, number of hidden layers or neurons, number of iterations, activation choice) are chosen by you before training and tuned to learn good parameters.
questions.explain: Also mention the loop: Idea → Code → Experiment.

questions.q: What is the role of the train, dev and test sets?
questions.answer: Train: learn parameters. Dev: tune hyperparameters and compare models. Test: final unbiased estimate of performance. All should come from the same distribution.
questions.explain: With small datasets, k-fold cross-validation can replace a fixed dev set.

questions.q: In the lab, why does too large a learning rate (for example 50) degrade results while 0.001 also fails?
questions.answer: Too small: the steps are tiny, the cost stays near 0.693 and many more iterations are needed. Too large: the steps overshoot, the cost oscillates and ends higher (70% accuracy at lr 50). Choose the largest rate that keeps the cost decreasing smoothly.
questions.explain: Remember that lr 0.01 with 50000 iterations reaches 88%, so a small rate is slow, not broken.

questions.q: Why is ReLU the usual default for deep networks but the worst choice in the small flower network?
questions.answer: ReLU is piecewise linear, so its boundaries are straight segments with corners. With only 4 units there are too few segments to model the petals, and with small initialization many units are inactive. In deep networks the many layers compensate, and ReLU avoids saturation.
questions.explain: It needs He initialization and a smaller learning rate to perform well.

questions.q: Why is training accuracy alone not enough to choose the number of hidden units?
questions.answer: Training accuracy cannot detect overfitting: larger networks lower the training cost while accuracy plateaus at about 90%. A dev set is needed, and the best choice is the smallest size that generalizes well (here 3 to 5).
questions.explain: Mention extra computation as another cost of bigger layers.

questions.q: The input layer is counted when we say a network is a "2-layer neural network".
questions.explain: Only the hidden layers and the output layer are counted. A 2-layer NN has one hidden layer and one output layer.

questions.q: A neural network with only linear activations, however deep, is equivalent to a single linear layer.
questions.explain: The composition of linear functions is linear, so extra layers add nothing.

questions.q: The test set can be used to tune the learning rate as long as the dev set is small.
questions.explain: Tuning must be done on the dev set. Using the test set for tuning would make its estimate biased.

questions.q: A network has 3 input features, 5 hidden neurons and 1 output neuron. What is the shape of W[2]?
questions.explain: W[2] has shape (n_y, n_h) = (1, 5). Option A is the transposed shape and a common mistake.

questions.q: Which activation is most suitable for the hidden layers of a deep network by default?
questions.explain: ReLU is the most used default in deep networks. Sigmoid saturates (derivative at most 0.25) and a linear activation collapses the network.

questions.q: At the start of training with small random weights, the cross-entropy cost for binary classification should be about:
questions.explain: a[2] ≈ 0.5, so the cost is about -log(0.5) ≈ 0.693.

questions.q: Which of the following are hyperparameters? (select all)
questions.explain: W[1] is learned, so it is a parameter. The others are chosen before training.

questions.q: Which statements about the backward pass of the 1-hidden-layer network are correct? (select all)
options: The * in dZ[1] is element-wise multiplication
questions.explain: dW[1] = (1/m) dZ[1] Xᵀ, not A[1]ᵀ. A[1]ᵀ is used for dW[2].

questions.q: Explain the symmetry problem and how it is solved.
questions.answer: If all weights are initialized to zero (or equal), every hidden neuron computes the same output and receives the same gradient, so they remain identical and the layer acts like one neuron. Random initialization of W breaks the symmetry.
questions.explain: Biases can start at zero without causing this problem.

questions.q: Using the lab's hidden layer experiment, explain why n_h = 4 is a good choice for the flower dataset rather than n_h = 50.
questions.answer: n_h = 1-2 underfits (about 67%), while n_h = 3-5 jumps to about 90%. For n_h ≥ 10 accuracy stays about 90% while computation and overfitting risk grow, so we pick the smallest size that generalizes well.
questions.explain: Note that this experiment uses training accuracy, so a dev set would be needed to confirm.
